title: Rocks: hard and soft rocks, what we use them for, and how pebbles get round

summary.text: A pebble from a river is smooth and round, but a freshly broken stone has sharp corners. What made the pebble round? Rocks are made of tiny grains called minerals, and some rocks are much harder than others. People choose each rock for a job: hard granite for steps and grinding stones, soft chalk for writing, marble for floors. Your child shakes chalk, salt and stone pieces in a steel tiffin to see which ones lose their corners, and tests rocks with a fingernail, a coin and a key. Last, we ask what happens to a hill or a river when people dig rock and sand out of it.
summary.art: A girl on a flat balcony holding a round grey pebble in one hand and a sharp chip of stone in the other, with a steel tiffin box and a chalk stick on the floor beside her.

intro.hook: A broken stone has sharp corners. A river pebble is smooth and round. What made the pebble round?
intro.text: Hold a pebble from a plant pot, if you have one. Run your finger over it. There are no sharp corners at all. Now look at a stone chip, or a broken piece of tile. Its edges are sharp. Both are rock. In this unit you find out how a sharp rock can turn into a round pebble, and why some rocks wear away much faster than others. You also find out which rocks are in your home, and why people chose them.
intro.art: Two hands side by side: one holding a smooth round pebble, the other holding a sharp, broken stone chip, with a faint question mark between them.

outcomes: By the end I can say what a rock is, and that most rocks are made of tiny grains called minerals.
By the end I can name granite, marble, sandstone, slate and coal, and say one thing each is used for.
By the end I can test which rocks are hard and which are soft, using my fingernail, a coin and a key.
By the end I can explain, using my Tiffin Test, how a sharp rock slowly becomes a round pebble and then sand.
By the end I can say why a hard rock is good for steps and a soft one is good for writing.
By the end I can say how digging rock and sand out of hills and rivers changes the place for plants, animals and people.

terms.meaning: Rock is the hard, natural material that the ground is made of, under the soil and the sea. It was not made by people.
terms.example: The big boulders at Hampi in Karnataka are rock. So is the grinding stone in many kitchens.
terms.art: A child standing beside a giant round boulder, with smaller rocks and a grinding stone shown in small circles around her.

terms.meaning: A mineral is a natural material that is the same all the way through. Most rocks are made of grains of a few minerals packed together.
terms.example: Salt is a mineral. Quartz, the glassy grains in granite and in most sand, is a mineral too.
terms.art: A close-up of a piece of granite, with its black, white, pink and glassy grains drawn large and labelled 'minerals'.

terms.meaning: A hard rock is not scratched or worn away easily. A soft rock can be scratched with a fingernail or a coin, and rubs away quickly.
terms.example: Granite is hard, so it is used for temple steps. Chalk is soft, so it leaves a line on a board.
terms.art: On the left, a granite step with no marks. On the right, a chalk stick leaving a white line on a black slate.

terms.meaning: A pebble is a small, smooth, rounded piece of rock. Water rolled it against sand and other stones until its corners wore off.
terms.example: The round stones on the bed of the Kaveri river, or in the bottom of a plant pot, are pebbles.
terms.art: A handful of smooth pebbles of different colours on a child's palm, with a river in the background.

terms.meaning: To wear away means to lose tiny bits, a little at a time, by rubbing or knocking. When wind, water or ice does this to rock, scientists call it erosion.
terms.example: An old grinding stone gets a smooth dip in the middle, because the grinding wears it away.
terms.art: An old grinding stone with a smooth hollow in the middle, and a few grains of dust beside it.

terms.meaning: Granite is a hard, speckled rock. It formed deep underground from melted rock that cooled very slowly.
terms.example: The Brihadeeswarar temple in Thanjavur is built of granite. Many kitchen counters are granite too.
terms.art: A tall temple tower of grey granite, next to a polished speckled kitchen counter.

terms.meaning: Marble is a smooth rock, often white, that can be cut and polished until it shines. It is softer than granite.
terms.example: The Taj Mahal is built of white marble from Makrana in Rajasthan.
terms.art: A white marble floor that shines, with a small drawing of the Taj Mahal above it.

terms.meaning: A quarry is a big open pit where people dig or cut rock out of the ground.
terms.example: Kota stone, used for floors in many homes, comes from quarries near Kota in Rajasthan.
terms.art: A wide pit with stepped grey sides, a digging machine and a truck, and a line of trees at the top edge.

explanations.definition: A rock is a hard, natural, solid material, usually made of grains of one or more minerals packed together.
explanations.description: The ground under the soil and the sea is rock. In some places it pokes up as hills and boulders. Look closely at most rocks and you see small grains packed tight. Each kind of grain is a mineral. Granite has black, white, pink and glassy grains, so it is made of several minerals. A brick looks like rock, but people made it by baking clay, so it is not a natural rock.
examples: Granite, with its specks of many colours.
Sendha namak, rock salt dug out of mines, for example near Mandi in Himachal Pradesh.
Sand on a beach, which is rock broken into tiny grains.
explanations.context: This card is about what a rock is, and the tiny grains that most rocks are made of.
explanations.art: A grey rock with a magnifying glass over one part, showing many small coloured grains packed together inside the circle.

explanations.definition: A harder material can scratch a softer one. A softer material cannot scratch a harder one.
explanations.description: To find out how hard a rock is, try to scratch it. Your fingernail scratches chalk. A steel coin scratches marble, but not granite. Most pebbles are so hard that a steel key leaves only a grey line of metal on them, which wipes off. Quartz, a glassy mineral in granite and many pebbles, is harder than steel. In 1812 a German scientist named Friedrich Mohs used this scratch idea to put ten minerals in order, from soft talc to hard diamond.
examples: A fingernail scratches a chalk stick.
Nothing at home scratches a quartz pebble, except another quartz pebble or something harder.
explanations.context: This card is about how we tell a hard rock from a soft one, by scratching.
explanations.art: Three small pictures in a row: a fingernail scratching chalk, a coin scratching marble, and a key sliding over a pebble with no scratch.

explanations.concept: Why we use each rock for its job
explanations.definition: People choose a rock for a job by what the rock is like: hard or soft, smooth or rough, full of holes or tightly packed, pretty or plain.
explanations.description: People choose a rock for a job by what the rock is like. Steps and grinding stones need hard granite that does not wear away fast. Chalk is soft, so it rubs off onto a board and leaves a line. Slate splits into thin flat sheets and keeps water out, so it was used for roofs and writing slates. Marble can be polished until it shines, so it is used for floors and statues. Coal is a black rock that burns, so it is used as fuel in power stations.
examples: Granite for the Brihadeeswarar temple in Thanjavur and for grinding stones.
White marble from Makrana for the Taj Mahal.
Red sandstone for the Red Fort in Delhi.
Red laterite blocks for houses in Kerala, Goa and the Konkan coast.
Slate from Markapur in Andhra Pradesh, once used for school slates.
Coal from mines in Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh.
explanations.context: This card is about why people pick a different rock for each job.
explanations.art: A grid of six small pictures: granite temple steps, a marble floor, a chalk stick on a board, a slate roof, a red laterite wall, and a lump of coal glowing in a fire.

explanations.concept: How a sharp rock becomes a round pebble, and then sand
explanations.definition: Rock wears away when it is knocked and rubbed. Corners stick out, so they are knocked most and wear off first.
explanations.description: Rock breaks off a hill as sharp pieces. Rain carries some into a stream. The water rolls them and bangs them against sand and other stones. Each knock takes off a few tiny grains, and the corners get knocked most. Slowly the piece turns round and smooth. Now it is a pebble. Soft rocks get round fast and break into sand. Hard rocks take a very long time. In the Tiffin Test, you shake chalk pieces in a steel tiffin and see them lose their corners in a few minutes.
examples: Round stones on the bed of the Kaveri, the Narmada or the Brahmaputra.
Smooth pebbles on the beach at Kanyakumari.
The sand at the edge of a river, which is rock in tiny grains.
explanations.context: This card is about how a sharp rock turns into a pebble, and a pebble into sand.
explanations.art: Four pictures in a line along a river: a sharp rock breaking off a mountain, a rough stone in a stream, a smooth pebble lower down, and sand at the sea.

explanations.concept: Digging rock and sand out of the land
explanations.description: People dig rock out of quarries and scoop sand from river beds to build homes, roads, bridges and schools. A quarry can turn a hill with trees into a deep pit. The birds, insects and other animals who lived there lose their home. Too much sand taken from a river makes the river bed deeper. Then the banks can fall in and nearby wells can dry up. People argue about how much digging is fair.
examples: Granite quarries in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.
Sand taken from river beds for building in many states.
An old quarry that has filled with rain and become a lake, where birds now come.

perspectives.explanation: Families need homes and children need schools. Stone and sand are the best materials we have, so we must dig them.

perspectives.who: A farmer who lives by the river
perspectives.explanation: When too much sand is taken, the river bank falls in and my well dries up. Dig less, and only in some places.
A river brings new sand down each year, but slowly. If we take out more than the river brings, the river bed sinks. We should measure, and take less than that.

explanations.context: This card is about what happens to hills and rivers when people dig rock and sand out of them, and why people disagree.
explanations.art: Two pictures side by side: a green hill with trees and birds, and the same place as a stepped grey quarry pit with a truck.

agreed.text: Most rocks are made of grains of minerals packed together.
agreed.evidence: Under a magnifying glass, granite shows separate grains of different colours. Broken or ground rock falls apart into grains like these.
agreed.context: This card is about what scientists agree rocks are made of.

agreed.text: A harder mineral scratches a softer one, never the other way round.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can test it with a fingernail, a coin and a key. Scientists have used this test since Friedrich Mohs listed ten minerals by hardness in 1812.
agreed.context: This card is about how scientists tell hard rocks from soft ones.

agreed.text: Pebbles and sand are made when moving water, wind or ice knock and rub rock.
agreed.evidence: Stones in rivers are rounder further downstream. Rock pieces shaken or rolled in a drum turn round, just as in the Tiffin Test. Most sand grains, looked at closely, are tiny bits of rock.
agreed.context: This card is about what scientists agree makes pebbles and sand.

challenging.claim: Rocks never change. A rock stays the same for ever.
challenging.for: A rock looks the same this year as last year. Old temples of stone are still standing after a thousand years.
challenging.against: Old grinding stones get a dip in the middle, old steps get worn smooth, and river stones turn round. The change is just too slow to see in one day.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that rocks never change.

challenging.claim: A heavier stone is always harder.
challenging.for: Big heavy stones feel strong. Heavy things often feel tough.
challenging.against: Hardness depends on the mineral grains, not on the size. A big lump of chalk is heavy but soft. A tiny grain of quartz sand is light but harder than steel.
challenging.context: This card is about whether heavy rocks are harder rocks.

challenging.claim: Taking sand from a river does no harm, because the river brings more sand every year.
challenging.for: Rivers really do carry new sand down from the hills, especially in the monsoon.
challenging.against: Rivers bring new sand slowly. In many Indian rivers, more sand has been taken than the river brings, and the river beds have sunk.
challenging.context: This card is about whether taking sand from rivers harms them.

big_questions.q: If a river can turn a sharp rock round, what is the river doing to its own bed and banks all the time?
big_questions.hint: In the Tiffin Test, you shook chalk pieces in a steel tiffin. Was it only the chalk that wore away? What about the inside of the tiffin?

big_questions.q: Is a grain of sand a rock, or only a piece of one? When does a piece stop being a rock?
big_questions.hint: Think of chalk breaking into smaller and smaller bits. Is the dust still chalk?

big_questions.q: A hill took millions of years to form. A quarry can dig it away in a few years. Who should decide whether to dig it?
big_questions.hint: Think about the builder, the farmer, the birds on the hill, and the children who need a school.

big_questions.q: A grinding stone and a temple step wear away a little each day. Is anything in the world truly lasting?
big_questions.hint: Some changes are too slow to notice. Is slow change still change?

story.title: The Dip in Paati's Grinding Stone
story.note: Meenu, Paati and Selvi akka are made up. It is true that grinding stones are usually granite, that they wear smooth with use, and that people in many towns still go from house to house roughening them with a chisel. Pebbles in rivers like the Kaveri are rounded by being rolled against sand and other stones.
text: Meenu was seven, and she lived with her Paati in a flat in Madurai. Paati is the Tamil word for grandmother. On their balcony sat a heavy grey grinding stone, called an ammikal. Paati used it to grind coconut chutney, with a long round stone that rolled back and forth on top.
One morning Meenu looked closely at the ammikal. In the middle there was a smooth, shallow dip, like a very wide spoon. "Paati, who carved this dip?" she asked.

Paati laughed. "Nobody carved it. This ammikal belonged to my mother. Every day for sixty years, someone has ground chutney and masala on it. Each time, the stone loses a few tiny grains. Sixty years of grinding made that dip."
Meenu ran her finger across it. The stone felt hard, much harder than a brick. "But it is so hard. How can rubbing wear it away?"
"Ask Selvi akka," said Paati. "She is coming today."

Selvi akka came up the stairs after lunch. Akka means older sister, and it is a polite way to speak to a woman. She had a small cloth bag of tools, and she went from house to house making old grinding stones rough again. She sat down by the ammikal and took out a little chisel and a hammer. Tap, tap, tap. She made rows of tiny pits all over the smooth dip.
"Why are you making it rough, akka?" asked Meenu.

"A smooth grinding stone does not grip the coconut," said Selvi akka. "The grinding has polished it. The rough bits wore away, and now the top is too smooth. So every year or two I tap it rough again."
"Then it gets smaller every time," said Meenu.

"A little smaller, yes." Selvi akka held up a sharp chip that had flown off. "This is granite. Granite is one of the hardest rocks. Even so, rubbing wears it away, grain by grain. Softer rocks wear away much faster."

That evening Meenu took out the pebble Paati had brought her from the Kaveri river at Srirangam. It was grey and speckled, like the ammikal, and perfectly smooth. Next to it she put Selvi akka's chip. The chip had sharp corners that pricked her thumb.
"Paati, are these the same rock?"
Paati looked at them through her reading glasses. "They look like it. Both have the same specks."
"Then who made the pebble round?"
Paati smiled. "What do you think?"
Meenu thought about the chutney stone. Rubbing had made the dip. Maybe rubbing had made the pebble round too. But who had rubbed a stone in a river?
She fetched her box of chalk and broke one stick into five sharp pieces. She put them in Paati's small steel tiffin, closed the lid, and shook it hard. She counted a hundred shakes. Her arm ached.
When she opened the lid, white dust covered the inside of the tiffin. The chalk pieces had lost their sharp corners. They looked like tiny white pebbles.
"The knocking did it!" said Meenu. "The corners stick out, so they get knocked most."
Then she put Selvi akka's granite chip in the tiffin and shook it a hundred times. It came out exactly as sharp as before.
"Granite is too hard for a hundred shakes," said Paati.

Meenu looked at her river pebble. It had the same specks, so it looked like granite too, and it was completely round. "Then the Kaveri must have rolled it for years and years," she said slowly. "Bumping it on sand and other stones, every day, all the way down from the hills."
"Every monsoon," said Paati. "Every flood. Far longer than you or I have been alive."

Meenu held the pebble in one hand and the sharp chip in the other. They were the same rock. One had stayed still, and one had travelled a long way. She put the pebble on the balcony wall, next to the ammikal, where she could see them both.
story.epiphany: Meenu sees that rubbing and knocking wear away even hard granite, a few grains at a time. Her chalk turned round in a hundred shakes, but the granite chip did not change. So her round granite pebble must have been rolled by the river for a very long time.
ask: Who made the dip in Paati's ammikal?
Why did Selvi akka tap the stone to make it rough?
Why did the chalk turn round in the tiffin, but the granite chip did not?
How did Meenu work out that her pebble had travelled a long way?
art: A girl and her grandmother on a flat balcony, looking at a grey grinding stone with a smooth dip in the middle.
A woman with a cloth bag of tools tapping tiny pits into a grinding stone with a small chisel and hammer, while the girl watches.
A girl holding a smooth speckled pebble in one hand and a sharp speckled chip in the other.
A girl opening a steel tiffin full of white dust and small rounded chalk pieces, smiling.

games.title: Rock Job Match: which rock for which job?
games.context: In this memory game you find pairs: a rock card and the job that suits that rock. To keep a pair, you must say why the rock suits the job.

printables.title: 8 rock cards to cut out
items: Marble: smooth, can be polished to shine
Chalk: very soft, rubs off easily
Slate: splits into thin flat sheets, keeps water out
Sandstone: made of sand grains stuck together, easy to carve
Laterite: red, full of small holes, easy to cut into blocks
Rock salt: a rock you can eat

printables.title: 8 job cards to cut out
items: Temple steps that millions of feet walk on
A floor that shines like a mirror
Writing a sum on a blackboard
A roof that keeps the rain out
A big red fort with carved walls
Cheap, strong blocks for a house wall near the sea
Salt for a dish cooked during a fast

rules: Cut out the 16 cards. Mix them up and lay them face down in 4 rows of 4.
On your turn, turn over two cards and read them aloud.
If one is a rock and the other is the job that suits that rock, say why it suits the job. The pair list in the grown-up note below tells you which cards go together.
If your reason fits, keep the pair and have another turn. If it does not fit, or the cards do not match, turn them face down again. The next player has a turn.
When all the cards are matched, the player with the most pairs wins. If two players have the same number, they both win.

setup.art: Sixteen small cards laid face down on a floor in four rows of four.
setup.caption: 1. Lay all 16 cards face down in 4 rows.

setup.art: A child turning over a card that says 'Chalk' and another that says 'Writing a sum on a blackboard', smiling.
setup.caption: 2. Turn over two cards. Is it a rock and its job?

setup.art: The child holding the pair and talking, with a grown-up nodding.
setup.caption: 3. Say why the rock suits the job, and keep the pair.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards together. 2. Read every rock card aloud once. 3. Mix all 16 cards and lay them face down.
flow.say: Here are eight rocks and eight jobs. Let us read the rock cards first. Then we hide them all.
flow.kid: Read the rock cards. Then turn all the cards face down.

flow.do: 1. Take turns turning over two cards. 2. When a pair matches, ask for the reason. 3. Keep score on the sheet.
flow.say: Is that a rock and its job? Why does this rock suit this job?
flow.kid: Turn over two cards. Is it a rock and its job? Say why.

ask.q: Why is chalk good for writing on a board?
good: It is soft, so it rubs off and leaves a line.
Bits of it stay on the board.

flow.parent: The pairs: granite and temple steps (hard, does not wear away); marble and the shiny floor (polishes to a shine); chalk and writing on a board (soft, leaves a line); slate and the roof (thin flat sheets, keeps water out); coal and fuel (burns); sandstone and the red fort (easy to carve); laterite and house walls near the sea (cut into blocks); rock salt and salt for cooking. A good reason names what the rock is like: hard, soft, shiny, flat sheets, burns. 'Because it is chalk' is not yet a reason.

flow.do: 1. Count the pairs. 2. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Let us count the pairs. Now, one last question for everyone.
flow.kid: Count your pairs. Then answer the question.

check.q: Why are temple steps made of granite and not chalk?
options: Granite is hard, so feet do not wear it away fast
check.why: Granite is very hard, so millions of feet wear it away only very slowly. Chalk is soft and would soon wear into dust.

games.title: The Hill Meeting: should we dig this hill?
games.context: In this talking game, a company wants to dig a rocky hill into a quarry. Each player speaks for someone who cares about the hill. At the end, everyone votes on a plan.

items.b: You need granite to build 200 new flats and a school. Without stone, families have nowhere to live.

items.f: The woman who grazes goats on the hill
items.b: Your goats eat the grass on the hill every day. Where will they eat if the hill becomes a pit?

items.f: A peahen who nests on the hill
items.b: You lay your eggs in the bushes on the hill. The noise and the digging will scare you away.

items.f: A girl who goes to the village school
items.b: Your school is old and the roof leaks. A new school would need stone. But you love climbing the hill.

items.f: A scientist who studies the land
items.b: You know the rain soaks into the hill and fills the village wells. A deep pit could change where the water goes.
This gives the most stone, the fastest. The hill is gone.

items.f: Plan 2: Do not dig at all.
items.b: The hill stays. The builder must bring stone from far away, which costs more.

items.f: Plan 3: Dig one side only, and plant trees there afterwards.
items.b: This gives some stone. Part of the hill stays. It takes longer.

rules: Each player takes a role card. With fewer than 5 players, share out all five role cards so that every role is spoken for.
Turn your role card over and read what you care about. A grown-up can read it to you.
Take turns. Say who you are and what you want for the hill, in one or two sentences.
Then lay out the three plan cards. Read the front of each one aloud, then turn it over to read what it would mean. Everyone talks about which plan is fairest.
Each player votes for one plan by putting a finger on it. Count the votes. If two plans tie, talk for one more minute and vote again.
Last, each player says one thing another player said that they agree with.

setup.art: Five role cards laid out in a fan: a builder, a woman with goats, a peahen, a schoolgirl, and a woman scientist with a notebook.
setup.caption: 1. Each player takes a role card.

setup.art: Three plan cards in a row on a mat, with children's fingers pointing at different ones.
setup.caption: 2. Talk about the three plans, then vote.

flow.do: 1. Hand out the role cards. 2. Help each player read theirs.
flow.say: A company wants to dig this hill for stone. Each of you speaks for someone who cares about the hill.
flow.kid: Take a card. That is who you are today.

flow.do: 1. Each player speaks in turn. 2. Lay out the plan cards. 3. Let everyone argue for a plan.
flow.say: Tell us who you are, and what you want for the hill. Which plan is fairest to everyone?
flow.kid: Say who you are. Say what you want for the hill.

ask.q: Who would lose the most if the whole hill was dug?
good: The peahen and the goats, because the hill is their home and food.
The village, if the wells dry up.

flow.parent: There is no single right plan. Praise a player who thinks of someone else, not only of their own role.

flow.do: 1. Everyone votes. 2. Count the votes. 3. Each player names one thing they agreed with.
flow.say: Put your finger on the plan you choose. Now say one thing someone else said that you agree with.
flow.kid: Vote for one plan. Then say one thing you agreed with.

check.q: Why does a builder want to dig the hill?
options: To get stone for homes and a school
check.why: Builders need hard rock like granite for walls, floors and roads. That is why quarries are dug.

experiments.title: The Tiffin Test: which rock pieces lose their corners?
experiments.context: In this experiment you shake sharp pieces of chalk, salt and stone in a closed steel tiffin, 100 shakes each. Then you look at which ones have lost their corners. This is a fast copy of what a river does to rocks.
experiments.question: If we shake sharp pieces of chalk, salt and stone the same way, which ones lose their corners and turn round?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which pieces will lose their corners after 100 shakes: the chalk, the salt or the stone? Which will not change at all? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Each kind is shaken in the same tiffin, 5 pieces at a time, for 100 hard shakes. The tiffin is tipped out and wiped between kinds. Only the kind of rock changes.
results_table: Dust in the tiffin: a lot, a little or none

materials.item: 1 stick of chalk, broken into 5 pieces with sharp corners
5 big salt crystals (kal uppu or khada namak), or a small lump of sendha namak broken into 5 pieces by a grown-up
5 small, sharp stone chips: gravel (jelly) from a building site or hardware shop, a granite offcut from a stone shop, or chips from a plant pot
1 round pebble, if you have one, to compare with
a small steel tiffin box or dabba with a tight lid
a sheet of dark paper, or a dark plate
a pencil and paper for the table

schedule.what: Guess. Draw one piece of each kind. Shake each kind 100 times. Look, draw again, and fill in the table. Talk about the river pebble.

experiments.record: Draw one piece of each kind before and after shaking. Fill in the table. Circle the kind that changed the most.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results (yours may differ)
rows: Corners rubbed round, a few crumbled bits

setup.art: Three small heaps on a dark plate: five sharp chalk pieces, five salt crystals, and five grey stone chips, with a round pebble beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Make three heaps of 5 sharp pieces.

setup.art: A child drawing one chalk piece on a sheet, showing its sharp corners.
setup.caption: 2. Draw one piece from each heap.

setup.art: A child holding a closed steel tiffin with both hands and shaking it hard up and down.
setup.caption: 3. Put one heap in the tiffin and shake it 100 times.

setup.art: An open steel tiffin with white dust inside and small rounded chalk pieces tipped onto dark paper.
setup.caption: 4. Tip the pieces onto dark paper and look at the corners.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the three heaps and the round pebble. 2. Let them feel the sharp corners. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write it down.
flow.say: These pieces all have sharp corners. Which ones will turn round after 100 shakes? Which will stay sharp? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Feel the sharp corners. Which pieces will turn round? Why?

ask.q: Which pieces do you think will lose their corners?
good: The chalk, because it is soft.
The stone, because it is heavy and bangs hard.
None of them, because they are all hard.

flow.parent: Write down any guess and say nothing yet. Some children think the heaviest pieces will change most. The test will answer it. Stone chips can have sharp edges, so keep a grown-up close, and wash hands afterwards.

flow.do: 1. Your child picks one piece from each heap. 2. They draw each one, showing its corners. 3. Put the pieces back.
flow.say: Draw one piece from each heap. Show its corners clearly. We will draw them again after shaking.
flow.kid: Draw one piece from each heap. Draw the corners.

flow.do: 1. Put the 5 chalk pieces in the tiffin and close the lid tightly. 2. Your child shakes it hard, counting to 100. 3. Tip the pieces onto the dark paper. 4. Wipe the tiffin and do the same with the salt, then the stone chips.
flow.say: Close the lid tight. Shake it hard, up and down, and count to 100. Now tip them out. Let us do the next heap the same way.
flow.kid: Shake the tiffin hard. Count to 100. Tip the pieces out. Do each heap the same.
flow.parent: It is noisy, and that is fine. Counting in tens helps. If small arms get tired, take turns, but shake every heap the same number of times so the test is fair.

flow.do: 1. Look at each heap on the dark paper. 2. Feel the corners. 3. Look at the dust left in the tiffin each time. 4. Your child draws the pieces again and fills in the table.
flow.say: Feel the corners now. Which pieces changed? How much dust did each one leave?
flow.kid: Feel the corners now. Which changed? Draw them again.

good: The corners went rounder and there was white dust.
It looks smaller and smoother than before.

check.q: Which pieces changed the least after 100 shakes?
check.why: Chalk and salt are soft, so each knock took off grains. The hard stone chips hardly changed.

flow.parent: Chalk usually loses its corners and makes white dust. Salt crystals may round a little or just crumble into grains, and either is fine. Stone chips stay sharp. Write down what you really see, even if it is not what you guessed.

flow.do: 1. Put a round pebble next to a sharp stone chip. 2. Ask the question and wait for an answer. 3. Ask what your child thinks, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: This pebble is hard stone too, and it is round. The chips did not change in 100 shakes. So how long must a river have rolled this pebble?
flow.kid: Look at the pebble and the chip. How did the pebble get round?

ask.q: How did the pebble get round?
good: A river rolled it and knocked it for a very long time.
It was knocked many, many more times than our 100 shakes.

flow.parent: A good answer has three parts. What I think: hard pebbles were knocked for a very long time. What I saw: chalk went round in 100 shakes, but stone did not. Why: hard rock loses grains very slowly. Some shop pebbles are rounded in a machine drum, which does the same knocking.
flow.think: The inside of the tiffin got knocked too. Did the tiffin wear away a little?

experiments.title: The Scratch Ladder: which rock is hardest?
experiments.context: In this experiment you try to scratch four kinds of rock with three tools: your fingernail, a steel coin and a steel key. A rock that is scratched by your fingernail is very soft. A rock that nothing scratches is very hard.
experiments.question: Which of our rocks can a fingernail scratch, which can a coin scratch, and which can nothing scratch?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which rock is the hardest, and which is the softest? Will the shiniest rock be the hardest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every rock is tested with the same three tools, pressed with the same firm push and dragged once. Only the rock changes.
results_table: Fingernail scratches it? yes or no
Coin scratches it? yes or no
Key scratches it? yes or no

materials.item: 4 rocks: a chalk stick, a lump of rock salt or a big salt crystal, a piece of marble or Kota stone (a free offcut from a stone shop, not a ceramic tile), and a pebble or a granite chip
a steel coin, such as a 1 rupee or 2 rupee coin
a steel key or a steel nail (not a yellow brass key, which is softer)
a magnifying glass, if you have one
an old cloth to wipe the rocks

schedule.what: Guess. Scratch each rock with fingernail, coin and key. Wipe and look. Fill in the table and put the rocks in order from softest to hardest.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then line the rocks up from softest to hardest and draw them in that order.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: No, only a grey metal line that wipes off

setup.art: Four rocks in a row on an old cloth: a chalk stick, a salt lump, a white marble piece and a grey pebble, with a fingernail, a coin and a key above them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the four rocks and the three tools.

setup.art: A child pressing the edge of a coin firmly across a piece of white marble.
setup.caption: 2. Press each tool firmly and drag it once across each rock.

setup.art: A child wiping a pebble with a cloth and looking at it through a magnifying glass.
setup.caption: 3. Wipe the rock and look closely: is there a scratch?

flow.do: 1. Show the four rocks. 2. Ask which is hardest and which is softest, and why. 3. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: Which rock is the hardest? Which is the softest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which rock is hardest? Which is softest? Why?

ask.q: Which rock do you think is hardest?
good: The marble, because it is shiny.
The pebble, because it is round and smooth.

flow.parent: Many children pick the shiniest rock. Write the guess and wait for the test.

flow.do: 1. Your child scratches each rock with a fingernail, pressing firmly. 2. Then with the edge of the coin. 3. Then with the tip of the key. 4. After each scratch, wipe the rock with the cloth and look.
flow.say: Press hard and drag the tool across the rock once. Now wipe the rock. Is there a groove, or powder? Rub your finger over it.
flow.kid: Scratch with your nail. Then the coin. Then the key. Wipe and look each time.
flow.parent: Do not test on the kitchen counter, the floor or the grinding stone. On a hard pebble, the key may leave a grey line. That is metal from the key, and it wipes off. The rock is not scratched. Pebbles are not all the same: if your pebble is scratched, it is a softer rock, and that is a good result to write down.

check.q: The key left a grey line on the pebble, but the line wiped off. What does that tell you?
options: A little metal rubbed off the key onto the pebble, so the pebble is harder than the key
check.why: A softer thing cannot scratch a harder one. The key lost a little metal on the pebble, so the pebble is the harder one.

flow.do: 1. Fill in the table. 2. Line the rocks up from softest to hardest. 3. Compare with the guess.
flow.say: Which one did even your fingernail scratch? Which one did nothing scratch? Put them in a line, softest first.
flow.kid: Fill in the table. Line up the rocks, softest first.

ask.q: Was the shiniest rock the hardest?
good: No, the marble shines but the coin scratched it.
The plain pebble was the hardest.

flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: the pebble is the hardest. What I saw: nothing scratched it, but the coin scratched the marble. Why: a harder thing scratches a softer one.

activities.title: Rock Jobs: why did someone choose this rock?
activities.context: In this activity you find rock that is doing a job in or near your flat. For each one, you work out what the job needs, and why that rock was chosen.

materials.item: a pencil and a sheet of paper with three columns: Where, Which rock, What the job needs

schedule.what: Find three to five rocks doing a job. For each, say what the job needs.

activities.record: A table of three to five rocks, each with where it is and what its job needs, like 'does not wear away' or 'easy to clean'.

setup.art: A child with a sheet of paper touching a speckled granite kitchen counter.
setup.caption: 1. Find a rock doing a job, like the kitchen counter.

setup.art: A child crouching by the stairs of a building, rubbing a smooth worn step with one hand.
setup.caption: 2. Look at the steps. Are they worn?

setup.art: A sheet with three columns, Where, Which rock, What the job needs, with three rows filled in with drawings.
setup.caption: 3. Write what each job needs.

flow.do: 1. Walk round the flat and the stairs together. 2. Look for the kitchen counter, the floor, the steps, a grinding stone, a window sill. 3. For each one, your child says where it is and guesses the rock, and a grown-up writes it down.
flow.say: Let us find rock that is doing a job. What is this counter made of? What about the steps?
flow.kid: Find rock doing a job. Tell a grown-up where it is.
flow.parent: Common answers: granite counters and steps, marble, Kota stone or Shahabad stone floors, a granite grinding stone, a slate or granite window sill. A guess is fine. Floor tiles that are not stone are made from baked clay.

flow.do: 1. For each rock, ask what the job needs. 2. Write the answer in the last column for your child. 3. Look at the steps for a worn, smooth part.
flow.say: What does a counter need to be? What would happen if the steps were made of chalk?
flow.kid: What does each job need? Say it, and a grown-up writes it down.

ask.q: Why is a kitchen counter often granite?
good: It is hard, so knives and pots do not scratch it.
It does not soak up water or oil, so it is easy to clean.
Hot pans do not hurt it.

activities.title: Specks in the Stone: a close look at granite
activities.context: In this activity you look very closely at a granite counter, floor or step, with a magnifying glass or a phone camera zoomed in. You count how many colours of grains you can see. Different colours usually mean different minerals.

materials.item: a granite counter, floor, step or pebble
a magnifying glass, or a phone camera zoomed in
a little water on a cloth
coloured pencils and paper

schedule.what: Look closely at granite. Count the colours of grains. Wet it and look again. Draw a small patch.

activities.record: A drawing of a small square of granite, about the size of a stamp, with each kind of grain coloured in.

setup.art: A child holding a magnifying glass over a speckled granite counter, with one eye close to the glass.
setup.caption: 1. Look closely at the granite.

setup.art: A child's drawing of a square full of black, white, pink and grey grains.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a small patch, and colour each kind of grain.

flow.do: 1. Look at the granite through the glass or the phone camera. 2. Count the colours of grains together. 3. Wipe it with a wet cloth and look again.
flow.say: How many colours of grains can you see? Now I will wet it. Can you see the colours better?
flow.kid: Look closely. How many colours of grains? Look again when it is wet.

ask.q: How many kinds of grain did you see?
good: Three or four: black, white, pink or grey, and some glassy ones.

flow.parent: Granite is mostly feldspar (white, cream or pink), quartz (grey and glassy) and dark minerals such as mica (black and shiny). Water makes the colours brighter. Some polished counters sold as granite are other speckled rocks, and that is fine for this activity.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws a small square of the granite. 2. They colour each kind of grain.
flow.say: Draw a small square of what you see. Colour each kind of grain. Different colours usually mean different minerals.
flow.kid: Draw a small square. Colour each kind of grain.

check.q: Why does granite have specks of different colours?
options: It is made of grains of different minerals
check.why: Granite is made of several minerals packed together. Different minerals usually have different colours, so we see specks.

activities.title: Rocks of India: make a map
activities.context: In this activity you make a map of India that shows where some famous rocks come from, and what people built with them.

materials.item: an outline map of India, traced from a school atlas, or drawn by hand as a big rough shape on a sheet of paper
a school atlas or a phone map, to find the places
the 7 labels below, cut out
glue and coloured pencils

printables.title: 7 rock labels to cut out
items: Granite: Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu. The Brihadeeswarar temple.
Granite boulders: Hampi, Karnataka. Temples and giant round rocks.
Laterite: Kerala and Goa. Red house walls.
Slate: Markapur, Andhra Pradesh. Writing slates.
Coal: Jharkhand. Fuel for power stations.
Marble: Makrana, Rajasthan. The Taj Mahal.
Rock salt: Mandi, Himachal Pradesh. Sendha namak.

schedule.what: Find each place on the map. Stick its label there. Draw a tiny picture of what was built.

activities.record: A map of India with seven rock labels in the right places.

setup.art: An outline map of India on a table with small paper labels and a glue stick beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the map and the labels.

setup.art: A child sticking a label on Tamil Nadu, with a tiny temple drawn beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Stick each label in its place and draw what was built.

flow.do: 1. Read each label aloud. 2. Find the place on the map together. 3. Your child sticks the label and draws a tiny picture.
flow.say: This one says granite, Thanjavur. Where is Tamil Nadu? Stick it there and draw a little temple.
flow.kid: Read a label. Find the place. Stick it on. Draw a tiny picture.

flow.do: 1. Look at the finished map. 2. Ask the question.
flow.say: Look at the whole map. Which rocks are in the south? Which are in the north and east?
flow.kid: Look at your map. Which rock is nearest to where you live?

ask.q: Why might old houses in Kerala be made of laterite and not marble?
good: Laterite is found right there, so it is easy to get.
Marble would have to come from far away.

flow.parent: Builders long ago mostly used the rock found nearby, because carrying stone far was very hard.

projects.title: My Rock Box: collect, test and label
projects.context: In this project you collect six rocks and rock-like things, test each one, and make a labelled rock box from an egg tray to show your family.

materials.item: an egg tray or a box with small sections
6 things: chalk, rock salt, a pebble, a stone chip, a piece of marble or Kota stone, and a piece of brick to compare
a spoon of water and a steel coin
small paper labels and a pencil

schedule.what: Collect the six things. Put one in each section of the tray.
Test each one: scratch with a coin, and put three drops of water on it. Does the water soak in or sit on top?
Write a label for each: its name, hard or soft, soaks water or not, and one use or one question. A grown-up can write the words your child says. Show the box to someone at home.

projects.record: A rock box with six labels. Each label says the name, hard or soft, soaks water or not, and one use or one question.

setup.art: An egg tray with six sections, each holding a different stone, salt lump, chalk or brick piece.
setup.caption: 1. Put one thing in each section.

setup.art: A child dropping water from a spoon onto a piece of brick, which turns dark.
setup.caption: 2. Test each one with a coin and three drops of water.

setup.art: The egg tray with a small paper label in front of each section.
setup.caption: 3. Write a label for each one.

flow.do: 1. Collect the six things together. 2. Put one in each section of the egg tray.
flow.say: Let us collect six things for your rock box. The brick is here to compare, because people made it from clay.
flow.kid: Collect six things. Put one in each hole of the tray.

flow.do: 1. Scratch each one with the coin. 2. Put three drops of water on each and watch for one minute. 3. Write down what happens.
flow.say: Does the coin scratch it? Now three drops of water. Does the water soak in, or sit on top as a round drop?
flow.kid: Scratch each one with a coin. Put three drops of water on it. Watch.

ask.q: Which ones soaked up the water?
good: The brick and the chalk turned dark and drank it.
The salt started to dissolve.
The pebble and the marble kept the drop on top.

flow.parent: Brick and chalk have tiny gaps between their grains, so water soaks in. Salt dissolves in water. Marble and most pebbles have their grains packed tight, so the drop sits on top.

flow.do: 1. Write a label for each thing, with your child saying the words. 2. Your child shows the box to someone at home.
flow.say: Write the name, hard or soft, soaks water or not, and one use. If you do not know a use, write a question instead. Then show someone your rock box and tell them one thing about each rock.
flow.kid: Write a label for each one. Show your rock box to someone.

challenges.title: The Fastest Pebble Maker
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. In the Tiffin Test, 100 shakes turned chalk pieces round. Your job is to find a way to make a chalk piece as round as you can in only 50 shakes.
challenges.problem: Make the roundest chalk pebble you can, from a sharp piece of chalk, in only 50 shakes.
constraints: Use only things you have at home.
Start each try with a sharp chalk piece of about the same size.
materials: a steel tiffin box and a plastic box
salt crystals, dry rice, or a spoon of sand
general: Shake harder, so each knock is stronger.
Put in more pieces, so they knock each other more.
Use a steel box instead of a plastic one, because steel is harder.
creative: Add a spoon of sand, dry rice or salt crystals, so the chalk is rubbed like rock in a sandy river.
Add a spoonful of water, the way a river has water, and see if it helps or not.
Roll the box on the floor instead of shaking it, the way a river rolls stones.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own way. Test it against one of the ideas above, with a fresh piece each time. Which gave the roundest pebble in 50 shakes?

setup.art: Two boxes side by side, one steel and one plastic, each with a sharp chalk piece inside and a small heap of rice beside one.
setup.caption: 1. Get ready two or three ways to try.

setup.art: Three chalk pieces lined up on dark paper, from sharp to quite round, with a child pointing at the roundest.
setup.caption: 2. Shake each 50 times, then compare the pieces.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem together. 2. Choose two or three ways to try. 3. Break a chalk stick into sharp pieces of the same size.
flow.say: We can shake only 50 times. How could we make the chalk rounder in fewer shakes?
flow.kid: You have only 50 shakes. How can you make the chalk roundest?

flow.do: 1. Try each way with a fresh chalk piece. 2. Shake exactly 50 times each. 3. Lay the pieces in a row on dark paper.
flow.say: Use the same size of piece and the same 50 shakes each time. Only the way changes. Then we line the pieces up.
flow.kid: Try each way. Shake 50 times. Line up the pieces.
flow.parent: Sand is made of hard quartz grains, so it should rub chalk round fastest, like sand in a river. Rice and salt are softer and may help less. Try each and see.

flow.do: 1. Compare the pieces. 2. Ask why the winner worked.
flow.say: Which piece is roundest? Why do you think that way worked best?
flow.kid: Which piece is roundest? Why?

ask.q: Why might rice or salt help the chalk get round?
good: More hard bits knock and rub it.
Like sand in a river rubbing a stone.

items.p: Which of these is a natural rock?
items.why: Granite formed in the ground. People made the brick by baking clay, and the bead from plastic.

items.p: A piece of chalk is shaken many times in a closed tiffin with stone chips. Draw it before shaking and after shaking. Show the corners clearly.
items.a: A sharp-cornered piece, then a rounded piece with no sharp corners.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the corners going round, because the corners stick out and get knocked off first.

items.p: Draw a line from each word to what it means.
pairs: A small, smooth, round piece of rock
A material that the grains in a rock are made of
A big pit where people dig out rock
To lose tiny bits by rubbing or knocking
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: A pebble is rounded by water. Rocks are made of grains of minerals. A quarry is a pit dug for rock. Wearing away is losing tiny bits, a few at a time.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down. In the Tiffin Test, why did the chalk lose its corners but the stone chips did not?
items.a: Chalk is soft, so each knock took off grains. The stone is hard, so 100 knocks hardly took anything off.
items.why: A strong answer says soft rock loses grains with each knock, and hard rock loses them very slowly.

items.p: A big, heavy stone is always harder than a small one.
items.why: False. Hardness depends on what the rock is made of, not its size. A big lump of chalk is still soft.

items.p: Sort these into Hard rock and Soft rock.
items.a: see items
items.why: A coin scratches chalk and rock salt, so they are soft. Nothing at home scratches granite or a quartz pebble.

items.p: Two children are looking at a round pebble.

views.says: Somebody must have polished this pebble. Rocks are not round by themselves.
A river made it round, by knocking it against other stones for a long time.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use what happens when stones are knocked together again and again. Then say one thing the other child is right about.
items.a: The second child is right for river pebbles. But the first child has a point: some shop pebbles are rounded in a machine drum by people.
items.why: A strong answer uses knocking: soft chalk shaken in a tiffin goes round, so knocking in a river can make stone round. It also sees that people can do the same knocking in a machine.

items.p: Most rocks are made of tiny grains called ________.
items.a: minerals
items.why: Rocks are made of grains of minerals packed together, like the specks in granite.

items.p: Here is a river from the hills to the sea, with three stones in it. Write 1 on the sharpest stone, 2 on the middle one and 3 on the roundest.
items.a: 1 on the stone high in the hills, 2 on the one in the middle, 3 on the one near the sea.
items.why: The further a stone travels, the more it is knocked, so it gets rounder on the way down.
items.art: A river running from mountains on the left to the sea on the right, with a sharp stone near the mountains, a rough stone in the middle and a round pebble near the sea.

items.p: You shake chalk pieces in a tiffin. You count 20 shakes, then 20 more, then 20 more. How many shakes is that?
items.a: 60 shakes
items.why: 20 and 20 is 40. 40 and 20 more is 60.

worksheets.title: Hard, soft and where rocks come from (stretch)

items.p: In the Scratch Ladder, a coin scratched the marble but not the pebble. Which is harder?
items.why: A harder thing scratches a softer one. The coin could scratch the marble but not the pebble, so the pebble is harder.

items.p: Say it or write it. A grinding stone has a smooth dip in its middle. How did it get there?
items.a: Years of grinding rubbed away a few grains each day. All those grains together made the dip.
items.why: A strong answer says the stone wore away slowly, a little each time it was used.

items.p: Three of these are natural rocks. Which one was made by people?
items.why: People make bricks by shaping clay and baking it hot. Granite, marble and slate formed in the ground.

items.p: Draw a small patch of granite as it looks close up. Colour each kind of grain.
items.a: A square full of grains in three or four colours, such as black, white, pink and grey.
items.why: A strong drawing shows separate grains of different colours, because granite is made of several minerals.

items.p: A builder and a farmer are talking about sand taken from the river near their town.

views.says: We need sand to make cement for houses. The river brings more sand every year.
Since they took so much sand, the river bank has fallen in and my well is lower.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give a reason. Then say what the other person is right about.
items.a: Both are partly right. Houses need sand, and rivers do bring new sand. But if more is taken than the river brings, the river bed sinks and banks and wells suffer.
items.why: A strong answer sees the need on both sides, and says the amount matters: take less than the river brings.

items.p: Sand on a river bank is mostly tiny bits of rock.
items.why: True. Rock that is knocked and rubbed for a long time breaks into tiny grains. Most sand grains are bits of rock, often quartz.

items.p: Put these rocks in order, from softest to hardest.
items.why: A fingernail scratches chalk, a coin scratches marble, and nothing at home scratches quartz.

items.p: Why is slate good for a roof?
items.a: Slate splits into thin flat sheets, and it keeps water out.
items.why: A strong answer names both things: flat thin sheets, and keeping rain out.

items.p: Draw a line from each rock to where it comes from in India.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These are well-known places for each rock. Builders long ago mostly used rock from nearby.

items.p: Someone says a quarry does no harm because it is only rock. What did they forget?
opts: Plants and animals lived on the hill, and lose their home
items.why: A hill is a home for plants, birds, insects and other animals. Digging a quarry takes that home away.

items.p: In the Tiffin Test, chalk turned round in 100 shakes but stone chips did not. A river pebble made of stone is round. What does that tell you about the pebble?
items.a: The pebble was knocked many, many more times than 100. A river must have rolled it for a very long time.
items.why: A strong answer uses the evidence: hard stone needs far more knocks than chalk, so a round stone pebble has been knocked for a very long time.

items.p: A child and her grandmother are talking about rocks.

views.says: Rocks never change. This temple is a thousand years old and looks the same.
Rocks do change. Our grinding stone has a dip worn into it, and the river made pebbles round.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use evidence. Then say what the other person is right about.
items.a: The child is right that rocks change, but her grandmother is right that hard rock changes very slowly, too slowly to see in a lifetime.
items.why: A strong answer uses evidence of wearing (the dip, the pebbles, the Tiffin Test) and also agrees that granite changes so slowly a temple can last a thousand years.

items.p: You want a step that will last 500 years. Which rock should you choose?
items.why: Granite is very hard, so feet wear it away very slowly. Chalk and rock salt are soft, and salt dissolves in rain.

items.p: A soft rock is bad for steps. Name a job where being soft is just what we want, and say why.
items.a: Writing on a board with chalk. The chalk is soft, so it rubs off and leaves a line.
items.why: A strong answer sees that soft is not bad. Each job needs something different.

items.p: Design a test to find out whether salt crystals or chalk pieces get round faster. Draw your test and label what you keep the same.
items.a: A drawing of two tiffins, the same number of pieces, the same number of shakes, with labels.
items.why: A strong design changes only the kind of piece, and keeps the box, the number of pieces and the shakes the same.

items.p: If a steel key leaves a grey line on a pebble, the key has scratched the pebble.
items.why: False. The grey line is metal rubbed off the key, and it wipes away. The pebble is harder than the key.

items.p: Here is a granite step outside an old temple. Label the part that has worn most, and say why.
items.a: The middle of the step is worn into a smooth dip, because most feet tread there.
items.why: A strong answer finds the dip and links it to the place where most feet rub.
items.art: An old stone temple step, with a smooth hollow worn in the middle and sharp edges still at the two ends.

items.p: An old quarry has filled with rain water. Birds now come to drink. What is true?
opts: Digging changed the place. It lost one home and later became a different one
items.why: The hill and its life were lost when it was dug. Later, rain filled the pit and some new life came. Both changes are real.

items.p: Sort these into Wears away fast and Wears away very slowly.
items: a lump of rock salt in the rain
items.a: see items
items.why: Soft chalk rubs away fast, and salt dissolves in water. Granite and quartz are hard, so they lose grains very slowly.

items.p: Name one place in your home or street where rock is slowly wearing away. How can you tell?
items.a: For example: the dip in a grinding stone, or a worn step. The middle is smooth and low where it was rubbed most.
items.why: A strong answer names a real place and what it looks like when rock has been rubbed for years.

videos.title: Why rocks are smoother near rivers
videos.why: Shows stones rolling in a fast river and getting rounder downstream. This takes years, so a child cannot watch it happen at home.
videos.check: Found by search: "Geology - Why Rocks Are Smoother Near Rivers." by TheGeoScholar, 2 minutes 54 seconds. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: How granite is mined in a quarry
videos.why: Shows how big blocks of rock are cut from the ground, and what a quarry does to the land.
videos.check: Found by search: "How Is Granite Mined? | Inside the Granite Quarry" by Stone Galleria LLP, 2 minutes 20 seconds. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: What minerals are in granite?
videos.why: Names the minerals that make up granite, so a child can match them to the grains seen in a real piece.
videos.check: Found by search: "Rocks & Minerals : What Is the Mineral Content of Granite?" by ehow, 2 minutes 59 seconds. A parent may preview it.

quiz.p: What are most rocks made of?
quiz.why: Most rocks are grains of minerals packed tight, like the specks in granite. 'Hard mud' is a common guess, but only some rocks start as mud.

quiz.p: Your fingernail scratches a rock. What does that tell you?
quiz.why: A fingernail is quite soft. If it can scratch a rock, the rock is even softer, like chalk.

quiz.p: Soft chalk pieces and hard stone chips are shaken together in a closed tiffin box. Which lose their corners first?
opts: All pieces at the same speed
quiz.why: Chalk is soft, so each knock takes off grains. Hard stone loses grains very slowly, so it hardly changes.

quiz.p: Why are the corners of a rock the first part to wear away?
opts: They stick out, so they get knocked most
They are made of softer rock
The corners are always a different kind of rock
quiz.why: Corners stick out, so most knocks land on them. That is why pieces turn round, not just smaller.

quiz.p: Which rock is used for writing on a board?
quiz.why: Chalk is soft, so it rubs off onto the board and leaves a line. Granite is too hard, and coal is used for burning.

quiz.p: A builder wants a stone that can be polished till it shines white, for a great monument. Which rock fits best?
quiz.why: Marble can be polished till it shines. The Taj Mahal is built of white marble. Laterite is red and rough, and coal is black and crumbles.

quiz.p: Why is a grinding stone made of granite?
opts: Granite is hard, so it wears away slowly and does not crumble into food
Granite is soft and easy to grind
quiz.why: A grinding stone is rubbed every day. Hard granite wears away very slowly, so it lasts for many years.

quiz.p: A perfectly round stone pebble lies by a river. How did it get round?
opts: The river rolled it against sand and stones for a long time
quiz.why: Moving water knocks and rubs stones. Over a long time the corners wear off and the stone turns round.

quiz.p: A hill is dug into a quarry. Who loses something?
opts: The plants, birds and other animals who lived on the hill
Nobody, because it is only rock
quiz.why: A hill is a home. When it is dug away, the plants and animals living there lose their home. People nearby may lose grazing land or water too.

quiz.p: Why do people dig rock and sand out of the ground?
opts: To build homes, roads, schools and bridges
Because rocks are in the way of rain
quiz.why: Stone, sand and gravel are used for walls, floors, cement and roads. That is why quarries and sand mining exist.

quiz.p: The shiniest rock is always the hardest.
quiz.why: False. Marble can shine, but a steel coin scratches it. A plain grey pebble can be much harder.

applications: Builders choose hard granite for steps, floors and kitchen counters that must last.
Gravel and sand, which are broken rock, are mixed with cement to make concrete for flats and bridges.
Sandpaper and the rough stone used to sharpen knives work by rubbing grains off, like a river does.
Scientists look at how round the stones in old rock layers are, to tell whether a river once flowed there.
Rock salt and sea salt are the same mineral, and both are used in cooking.

open_questions.q: Exactly how long does a river take to turn a sharp stone into a round pebble?
open_questions.why_open: It depends on the rock, the river, the size of the stone and the floods. Scientists have measured it in some rivers, but there is no one answer.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of minerals are there that nobody has found yet?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know about 6,000 kinds of minerals, and new ones are named every year. Nobody knows how many are still to be found.

open_questions.q: How much sand can be taken from a river without harming it?
open_questions.why_open: It depends on how much sand each river brings down each year, which changes with the monsoon. In many rivers it has not been measured well.

maths.problem: In the Tiffin Test, the chalk went round after 100 shakes. The stone chips still had sharp corners after 100 shakes, and after 100 more. How many shakes did the stone get in all? Is that enough to make it round?
maths.answer: 200 shakes, and no, it was still sharp.
maths.explain: 100 and 100 more is 200. Even 200 shakes did not round the stone. So a round stone pebble must have been knocked many more times than that.
maths.context: This is about the Tiffin Test, where you shook sharp pieces of chalk, salt and stone in a steel tiffin.
maths.why_maths: Adding up the shakes shows that even 200 knocks did not change the stone. So a river must give a pebble many more knocks than that.

maths.problem: Here are three rocks from the Scratch Ladder. Chalk was scratched by all 3 tools. Marble was scratched by 2. The pebble was scratched by 0. Put them in order from softest to hardest.
maths.answer: Chalk, then marble, then the pebble.
maths.explain: The more tools that scratch a rock, the softer it is. Chalk was scratched by 3, so it is softest. The pebble was scratched by 0, so it is hardest. Marble, with 2, sits in the middle.
maths.context: This is about the Scratch Ladder, where you tried to scratch four rocks with a fingernail, a coin and a key.
maths.why_maths: Ordering the numbers turns a table of yes and no into a line of rocks from softest to hardest.

maths.problem: On a walk round the flat, you found rock doing 5 jobs. 3 were granite and the rest were marble. How many were marble? Draw a tally for each.
maths.explain: 5 take away 3 is 2. The tally for granite has 3 lines and the tally for marble has 2 lines. So this home uses more granite.
maths.context: This is about Rock Jobs, where you found rocks doing jobs in or near your flat.
maths.why_maths: A tally shows at a glance which rock our home uses most.

roots.context: We have shaken chalk and stone in a tiffin, scratched rocks and found rocks doing jobs. Now we ask what a pebble tells us about time, change and ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In the Tiffin Test, the chalk pieces turned round and dusty after 100 shakes. The hard stone chips kept their sharp corners. A hard river pebble is round too, so it was knocked far more than 100 times. So a smooth pebble tells us a river or the sea has rolled it for a very long time.
deep_truth.habit: We think of a rock as something that stays the same for ever. The Tiffin Test shows that even hard rock loses grains with every knock. So a pebble got its shape slowly, over a very long time.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Tiffin Test, soft chalk lost its corners in 100 shakes, while hard stone chips did not. Yet river pebbles of the same hard stone are completely round.

three.who_am_i: You are shaped by what happens to you, a little every day, like the pebble. Your bones also contain a mineral, made from calcium and phosphorus.
three.what_is_life: Life keeps changing slowly, often too slowly to notice in one day. A pebble shows that small changes add up.
three.what_is_this_world: The ground under your flat is rock that is always changing, breaking, rolling and turning into sand, and later into new rock.

roots.thread: Everything is conscious, and rock is part of that same awareness, in its own way, at its own slow pace. A hill, a pebble, a grain of sand and the sandstone of a fort are one rock at different moments of one long story. Rock breaks into pebbles, pebbles into sand, and sand pressed together becomes rock again. Plants and animals, including us, live on this rock for a while and change it too. Most scientists today say only beings with nerves have minds, and they see rocks as matter that follows the laws of physics.

teachings.teaching: Nothing in the world is softer than water. Yet nothing is better at wearing down what is hard and strong.
teachings.link: Water alone is soft, but a river carries sand and stones, and they wear even hard granite round.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka tells his son Shvetaketu that by knowing one lump of clay, you know everything made of clay. The pot and the lid are only names. The clay is what is real.
teachings.link: A hill, a pebble and a pinch of sand have different names, but they are the same rock in different sizes.

science.text: Sand on most beaches and river banks is rock broken into tiny grains, often quartz. Sand buried and pressed for a very long time becomes sandstone.
Some philosophers, called panpsychists, think even tiny bits of matter have some kind of experience. Nobody knows for sure.

other_view.who: Many scientists, and the Charvaka thinkers of ancient India
other_view.view: They say a rock is only matter, with no awareness of any kind. A pebble changes because it is knocked, and that is all there is to it.

practice.title: Hold a Pebble, Feel the River
practice.say: Hold a pebble in your hand and close your eyes. Feel how smooth it is. Run your thumb all the way round. Breathe in slowly while I count to four. Breathe out slowly while I count to four. Now think of the river that rolled this pebble, year after year. Take three slow breaths, and keep feeling the smooth stone.

how_we_found_out.context: People once thought the ground had always been the way it is now. This card tells the true story of a scholar who worked out how India's land was made by looking at its pebbles.
how_we_found_out.story: Long ago, many people thought the ground had always been the way it is now, made all at once. About a thousand years ago, a scholar named Al-Biruni travelled into India from Ghazni, in what is now Afghanistan. He learned Sanskrit and wrote a big book about India, finished around the year 1030. In it, he wrote about the stones in the ground. Near the mountains, the rounded stones were big. Further from the mountains, they were smaller. Near the sea, where the rivers flow slowly, there was only sand. He also noticed that people found rounded stones however deep they dug. Al-Biruni said these stones had been carried and rubbed by rivers. So the flat land of India, he wrote, had once been a sea, slowly filled up by what the rivers brought down. Today geologists agree with a big part of this. The great plain of North India is made of thick layers of sand, mud and pebbles, carried down from the Himalayas by rivers over a very long time.
how_we_found_out.who: Al-Biruni, a Persian scholar from Khwarazm in Central Asia, who lived and studied in India
how_we_found_out.when: Al-Biruni finished his book on India around 1030 CE.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought the ground had always been as it is now. Al-Biruni saw that rounded river stones, big near the mountains and small near the sea, showed the land had been built up slowly by rivers.

In The Hill Meeting, 2 players can now share all five roles, and ties in the vote are settled. Followed the Tiffin Test and Scratch Ladder in a flat: salt may crumble instead of rounding, so the check now asks which pieces changed least, the example result and a pebble that does get scratched are marked honestly, and the Kota stone is a stone offcut, not a tile.
